summary: For ages 8-9, this topic develops the habit of looking for known mathematical structure before grinding a procedure: splitting a multiplication like 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 (distributive property), explaining ×10 as a place-value shift (digits move one column left) rather than 'add a zero', and using the quadrilateral hierarchy (a square is a special rectangle) to inherit properties from category to subcategory. The partitioned area model is the central representation, making the distributive split visible as two sub-rectangles. Activities centre on learners partitioning, justifying and generalising the structural move, not just reaching a correct answer.
misconceptions: Uses 'multiplying by 10 adds a zero', which fails for decimals (2.5×10 read as 2.50)
Splits distributively but forgets to multiply the second part (7×13 = 7×10 + 3)
Refuses that a square is a rectangle because the names/looks differ, so properties don't transfer down the hierarchy
Treats each multiplication as needing the column algorithm, not looking for a decomposition that makes it easy

activities.title: Split the rectangle: 7×13 from two easy facts
steps: Face 7×13 drawn as a rectangle 7 tall and 13 wide; mark where to cut the width to make a friendly 10 and 3
Cut the rectangle into a 7×10 part and a 7×3 part and work out each: 70 and 21
Combine the two parts (70 + 21 = 91) and state the matching number sentence: 7×13 = 7×10 + 7×3
Explain in your own words why BOTH parts have to be multiplied by 7 (both sub-rectangles are 7 tall)
Try a different cut of 13 (for example 11 and 2, giving 7×11 = 77 and 7×2 = 14) and check you still reach 91; say which cut was easiest and why
activities.insight: A multiplication that feels hard can be assembled from two multiplications you already know; the distributive property shares the ×7 across every part of the 13, which is why both parts must be multiplied.

activities.title: Why ×10 shifts digits, not 'adds a zero'
steps: Place a number such as 36 in a place-value chart (tens and ones), then multiply by 10 and move each digit one column to the left, writing a 0 in the emptied ones place to read 360
Now push 2.5 through ×10 in the same chart: move each digit one column left to get 25, and notice that appending a zero would wrongly give 2.50 (the same value as 2.5)
State a rule in your own words: ×10 moves every digit one place left; 'add a zero' only looks right for whole numbers because a zero happens to fill the empty ones place
Repeat for ×100 (two columns left) with one whole number and one decimal
activities.insight: Multiplying by 10 (or 100) is a place-value shift of every digit; 'add a zero' is only a lucky special case for whole numbers and breaks for decimals.

activities.title: Nested shape families: a square is a special rectangle
steps: Sort a set of quadrilaterals into nested property sets so squares sit inside rectangles, which sit inside parallelograms
For a given square, list what must be true of it just because it is a rectangle (e.g. it has four right angles) — without measuring
Complete sentences of the form 'A square must have … because it is a rectangle' and 'A square must have … because it is a parallelogram'
Decide and justify: is every rectangle a square? Explain why the inheritance runs one way down the hierarchy
activities.insight: Subcategories inherit the properties of the categories that contain them, so knowing 'a square is a rectangle' lets you carry rectangle properties down without re-checking; but the reverse is not guaranteed.

activities.title: 'What do I already know that this is like?' — probing and generalising
steps: Work out 7×13 mentally using a fact you already know instead of the written column method, then talk through how you split it and why that split is allowed
Answer: could you have split 13 a different way and still got 91? Which split was easiest and why?
Generalise: how is splitting 7×13 like splitting 6×13 or 7×23? Describe the structural move you reused
Before any standard algorithm on a new product, pause and ask 'is there a number fact or shape fact I already know that this is like?'
activities.insight: Using structure is a deliberate, transferable habit: decompose into known parts and justify the decomposition, rather than defaulting to a procedure.

checkQuestion: Work out 7 × 13 in your head, using a fact you already know instead of the written column method. Talk me through how you split it up and why that's allowed.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a distributive decomposition justified structurally: '7×13 is 7×10 plus 7×3, that's 70 and 21, so 91 — I can split the 13 because multiplying is sharing out over the parts.' The justification, not the 91, is the target.
